title: W11. 바이브코딩 팁
W11. 바이브코딩 팁
W11. 바이브코딩 팁
text:
프롬프트의 3요소
좋은 프롬프트 = 역할 + 맥락 + 구체적 요청

나쁜 프롬프트
통계 분석 해줘
→ AI가 뭘 해야 할지 모름. 쓸모없는 결과가 나옴.


좋은 프롬프트 (주기적인 프롬프트 엔지니어링 follow-up 필요!! 3~6개월)
너는 임상통계 전문가야.

나는 올리고전이 환자 대상 SBRT 논문을 쓰고 있어.
데이터프레임 df_pt에 다음 변수가 있어:
- Age_Tx: 치료 시 나이 (연속형)
- Sex: 성별 (M/F)
- Primary: 원발 부위 (Colon, Rectum, Lung 등)
- Death: 사망 여부 (0/1)
- OS: 전체 생존 기간 (개월)
- size_cm: 종양 크기 (cm)
- PTVmean_BED10: PTV 평균 BED10 (Gy)

다음을 수행하는 R 코드를 작성해줘:
1. gtsummary로 Table 1 생성 (Death 기준 그룹 비교, p-value 포함)
2. 변수명은 논문용 라벨로 변환
3. results/Table1.docx로 저장






힌트프롬프트 작성 팁




colnames(df) 결과를 붙여넣기 — AI가 변수명을 정확히 알아야 함
변수 타입 명시 — 연속형/범주형/생존시간 구분
원하는 출력 형태 지정 — “Word로 저장”, “tiff 300dpi”, “forest plot” 등
패키지 지정 — “gtsummary로”, “survminer로” 등

title: W11. 바이브코딩 팁
text:
실전 워크플로우
바이브코딩의 현실적인 작업 흐름은 이렇습니다:
1. RStudio에서 rds 로드
2. AI가 만든 코드를 콘솔에 붙여넣기 & 실행
3. 에러 → 에러 메시지를 AI에게 복붙 → 수정 코드 받기
4. 중간 결과 확인 (head, str, plot 등)
5. 만족하면 .R 파일로 저장
6. input → output 구조의 스크립트 완성
핵심은 처음부터 완벽한 스크립트를 만들려 하지 않는 것입니다. RStudio 콘솔에서 한 줄씩 돌려보고, 중간 과정을 계속 트러블슈팅해서 최종적으로 동작하는 코드가 완성되면 그때 파일로 저장합니다.


① RStudio에서 데이터 로드 & 구조 파악

library(tidyverse)

indir  <- "examples/analysis/"
outdir <- "examples/analysis/"
resdir <- "examples/results/"

df_pt <- readRDS(paste0(indir, "w11_2_df_pt_processed.rds"))

# 이 결과를 복사해서 AI에게 붙여넣기
colnames(df_pt)
str(df_pt)




② AI에게 프롬프트 작성
colnames()과 str() 결과를 붙여넣고, 원하는 분석을 요청합니다.
위 데이터에서 생존분석을 해줘.

- Kaplan-Meier curve: Death/OS 기준, Multiplicity(single vs multiple)로 그룹 비교
- Log-rank test p-value를 그래프에 표시
- Risk table 포함
- survminer 패키지 사용
- 300 dpi tiff로 저장



③ AI가 준 코드를 콘솔에서 실행
AI가 생성한 코드를 한 블록씩 RStudio 콘솔에 붙여넣어 실행합니다.
이때 위에서 본 함수 + main 구조로 코드가 올 가능성이 높습니다.
그 경우 main()을 바로 실행하지 말고, 함수 정의부를 먼저 실행한 뒤 함수를 하나씩 테스트하세요.

library(survival)
library(survminer)

# Kaplan-Meier 적합
fit <- survfit(Surv(OS, Death) ~ Multiplicity, data = df_pt)

# KM 곡선
p <- ggsurvplot(
  fit,
  data = df_pt,
  pval = TRUE,
  risk.table = TRUE,
  xlab = "Time (months)",
  ylab = "Overall survival",
  palette = c("#2E86AB", "#A23B72"),
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)

print(p)




④ 에러가 나면?
에러 메시지를 그대로 복붙해서 AI에게 주면 됩니다.
이 코드를 실행했더니 다음 에러가 났어:

Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE) : 
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 54, 0, 108

고쳐줘.
→ AI가 Death가 factor라서 Surv()에서 인식 못하는 걸 잡아줌
이런 식으로 실행 → 에러 → AI에게 복붙 → 수정을 반복합니다.






중요무지성 에러 복붙의 함정



에러가 나면 바로 AI에게 던지고 싶지만, 그 전에 30초만 직접 확인하면 훨씬 효율적입니다.
왜? AI는 대화가 길어질수록 앞의 맥락을 잊습니다. 에러를 복붙하고 → AI가 부분 수정하고 → 또 에러 → 또 복붙… 이걸 반복하면 원래 깔끔했던 코드가 누더기가 됩니다. 한 번에 고칠 수 있는 걸 돌아돌아 가게 되는 거예요.
에러가 났을 때 먼저 해볼 것:
# 1. 모르는 함수가 나왔으면 도움말 보기
?survfit
?ggsurvplot
?tbl_summary

# 2. RStudio에서는 Help 탭에 함수 이름 검색해도 됨
#    → Arguments 섹션에서 각 인자가 뭘 받는지 확인
#    → Examples 섹션에서 실제 사용법 확인










도움말의 Arguments 섹션만 훑어봐도 “아, 이 인자에 숫자를 넣어야 하는데 문자를 넣었구나” 같은 단서를 바로 잡을 수 있습니다.
실전 예시:
# AI가 만든 코드에서 에러 발생
ggsurvplot(fit, pval.coord = "top-right")  # Error!

# ?ggsurvplot → pval.coord는 c(x, y) 숫자 벡터임을 확인
ggsurvplot(fit, pval.coord = c(0.1, 0.1))  # 해결 ✅
이렇게 본인이 1차로 걸러낸 뒤 AI에게 물어보면, AI도 정확한 맥락에서 답을 주기 때문에 수정이 한 번에 끝납니다.








힌트에러 대응 순서




에러 메시지 읽기 — 어떤 함수에서 터졌는지 확인
?함수명으로 용법 확인 — 인자 타입, 필수/선택 여부
그래도 모르겠으면 — 에러 + ?함수명에서 본 내용을 같이 AI에게 주기

이 코드에서 에러가 났어:
[에러 메시지]

?ggsurvplot 도움말을 보니 pval.coord는 
numeric vector를 받는 것 같은데, 
어떻게 고쳐야 해?
이렇게 주면 AI가 헛다리 짚을 확률이 크게 줄어듭니다.




⑤ 동작 확인되면 스크립트로 저장
콘솔에서 다 돌아가는 걸 확인했으면, 코드를 모아서 .R 파일로 저장합니다. 이때 상단에 input/output을 명시하고, 경로를 paste0()로 정리합니다.

# ===== 03_KM_plot.R =====
# Input:  analysis/2_df_pt_processed.rds
# Output: results/KM_OS.tiff, results/KM_OS.pdf

# ----- 디렉토리 -----
indir  <- "examples/analysis/"
resdir <- "examples/results/"

library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(survminer)

# 1. 데이터 로드
df_pt <- readRDS(paste0(indir, "w11_2_df_pt_processed.rds"))

# 2. KM fit
fit <- survfit(Surv(OS, Death) ~ Multiplicity, data = df_pt)

# 3. Plot
p <- ggsurvplot(
  fit,
  data = df_pt,
  pval = TRUE,
  risk.table = TRUE,
  xlab = "Time (months)",
  ylab = "Overall survival",
  palette = c("#2E86AB", "#A23B72"),
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)

# 4. 저장
tiff(paste0(resdir, "w11_KM_OS.tiff"), width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", res = 300)
print(p)
dev.off()

ggsave(paste0(resdir, "w11_KM_OS.pdf"), plot = print(p), width = 7, height = 5)

cat("✅ KM plot saved!\n")

Rscript 03_KM_plot.R






노트스크립트 상단에 Input/Output 적기



# Input:  examples/analysis/w11_2_df_pt_processed.rds
# Output: examples/results/w11_KM_OS.tiff, results/KM_OS.pdf
이렇게 적어두면 나중에 파일만 봐도 이 스크립트가 뭘 읽고 뭘 만드는지 바로 알 수 있습니다.

경고




Reference level 방향 — relevel(factor, ref = "baseline")을 빠뜨리는 경우 많음
환자 vs 병변 단위 혼동 — OS는 환자 단위, LFFS는 병변 단위
다중비교 보정 누락 — subgroup 여러 개 비교하면서 Bonferroni 안 하는 경우
결측치 처리 — 기본값이 na.rm = FALSE라 결과가 NA로 나올 수 있음
생존 시간/이벤트 뒤바꿈 — Surv(time, event) 순서 주의

이것들은 사람이 알아야 합니다. 우리가 W2-W3에서 직접 R 문법을 배운 이유입니다.

title: W8. DEG 결과 처리
text:
p-value: 귀무가설(H₀: 그룹 간 차이 없음) 하에서 그 결과가 우연히 관찰될 확률
다중검정 문제 (Multiple testing problem): 유전자 1만 개를 p < 0.05로 검정하면 우연히 유의해지는 결과가 약 500개 → 위양성(false positive)이 급격히 증가





Bonferroni: \(\alpha / n_{total}\) → 지나치게 보수적
FDR (거짓 발견율, False Discovery Rate): \(FDR = \frac{FP}{FP + TP}\)










“순위가 높을수록 엄격하게, 낮을수록 관대하게”

\[
FDR \leq \frac{n_{total} \cdot p_{cut}}{i} \leq \alpha(0.05)
\]
\[
p_{cut} \leq \frac{i}{n_{total}} \cdot \alpha
\]

보정된 p-value (padj) … (누적 최솟값을 적용) \[
p \times \frac{n_{total}}{i}
\]


##| eval: true
 
## BH 절차를 직접 구현
pvalues <- c(0.04, 0.001, 0.05, 0.0001, 0.2)
genes <- c("GeneA", "GeneB", "GeneC", "GeneD", "GeneE")
df <- data.frame(Gene = genes, P_raw = pvalues)
df <- df[order(df$P_raw), ]
m <- nrow(df)
alpha <- 0.05
df$Rank <- 1:m
df$BH_Threshold <- (df$Rank / m) * alpha
df$Pass <- df$P_raw <= df$BH_Threshold
df$padj_calc <- pmin(df$P_raw * (m / df$Rank), 1)
df$padj_final <- rev(cummin(rev(df$padj_calc)))

## R 내장 함수
df$R_function <- p.adjust(df$P_raw, method = "BH")

df





count가 낮은 유전자 → 통계적 유의성을 얻기 어려움
사전 필터링 → 전체 검정 횟수 n이 줄어듦 → 검정력 증가
DESeq2::results() 에서 padj가 NA로 나오는 경우:

count가 낮은 유전자 (독립 필터링으로 제외됨)
이상치 유전자 (Cook’s distance 기준)

title: W8. DEG 결과 처리
text:
2. DEG 결과 시각화






노트실습 데이터 내려받기



아래 파일을 R 프로젝트의 data/ 폴더에 저장하세요.



파일
링크




dds_DESeq2.rds
📥 내려받기






##| eval: false

dds <- readRDS('data/dds_DESeq2.rds')

res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "Tumor", "Normal"))


MA Plot (전체 조망)
















X축: 평균 발현량 (Mean Average, A), Y축: 로그 비 (M = log₂FC)
데이터의 치우침과 저발현 유전자의 LFC 과대추정을 확인
Y=0을 중심으로 대칭이어야 함
apeglm::lfcShrink(): 저발현 유전자의 LFC를 억제 (권장)


##| eval: false
## MA plot
plotMA(res, ylim = c(-10, 10), main = "Before Shrinkage")

## LFC 축소 (apeglm)
library(apeglm)
resLFC <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "condition_Tumor_vs_Normal", type = "apeglm")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plotMA(res, main = "Before Shrinkage", ylim = c(-5, 5))
plotMA(resLFC, main = "After Shrinkage (Recommended)", ylim = c(-5, 5))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))



Volcano Plot (유전자 선별)






X축: log₂(Fold Change), Y축: −log₁₀(보정 p-value)
|LFC|가 크고 p-value가 낮은 유전자를 찾아냄


##| eval: false

library(ggrepel)

res_df <- as.data.frame(resLFC) %>%
  rownames_to_column("gene_id") %>%
  mutate(is_significant = padj < 0.05 & abs(log2FoldChange) > 1)

p_thr <- 0.05; lfc_thr <- 1
vol_data <- res_df %>%
  mutate(diffexpressed = case_when(
    log2FoldChange > lfc_thr & padj < p_thr ~ "UP",
    log2FoldChange < -lfc_thr & padj < p_thr ~ "DOWN",
    TRUE ~ "NO"
  ))

ggplot(vol_data, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj),
                     color = diffexpressed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("DOWN" = "blue", "NO" = "grey", "UP" = "red")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-lfc_thr, lfc_thr), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(p_thr), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text_repel(data = head(arrange(vol_data, padj), 10),
                  aes(label = gene_id), color = "black") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Volcano Plot",
       x = "Log2 Fold Change", y = "-Log10 Adjusted P-value")



Heatmap (패턴 확인)






상위 유의 유전자들의 발현 패턴을 시각화
Case/Control 간 패턴을 살피고 이상치 시료를 찾아냄
vst/rlog 변환 → z-score 스케일링 적용


##| eval: false

library(pheatmap)

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)

## 상위 20개 DEG
top_genes <- res_df %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(log2FoldChange))) %>%
  head(20) %>%
  .$gene_id

mat <- assay(vsd)[top_genes, ]
df <- as.data.frame(colData(dds)[, c("gender", "condition")])

pheatmap(mat,
         scale = "row",            ## z-score
         show_rownames = TRUE,
         show_colnames = FALSE,
         annotation_col = df,
         cluster_cols = TRUE,
         main = "Top 20 DEGs Heatmap")

title: W8. DEG 결과 처리
section: 📝 8주차 과제: 단순 모형 vs. 짝지은 모형
text:
📝 8주차 과제: 단순 모형 vs. 짝지은 모형

1. DEG 개수 비교

단순 모형 (~ condition): 약 17,000개 DEG
짝지은 모형 (~ patient + condition): 약 15,700개 DEG

분산 분해 관점에서 보면: 짝지은 모형은 환자 효과를 따로 설명하므로, 단순 모형에서 condition의 몫으로 잘못 돌아갔던 환자 간 분산이 분리됩니다. 그 결과 일부 유전자는 유의성을 잃지만, 남은 DEG는 진짜 생물학적 신호를 반영할 가능성이 더 높습니다.


2. Gold Standard 유전자
TOP2A, SFTPA1, SFTPB, SFTPC, AGER 같이 잘 알려진 LUAD 표지 유전자로 두 모형 사이의 p-value 변화를 확인해 보세요.


3. 특정 유전자를 강조한 Volcano Plot

##| eval: false

## 특정 유전자 강조
highlight_genes <- c("TOP2A", "SFTPA1", "SFTPB", "SFTPC", "AGER")
highlight_data <- vol_data %>% filter(gene_id %in% highlight_genes)

ggplot(vol_data, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj),
                     color = diffexpressed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("DOWN" = "blue", "NO" = "grey", "UP" = "red")) +
  geom_point(data = highlight_data, color = "purple", size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(data = highlight_data,
                  aes(label = gene_id), color = "purple") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Volcano Plot (Paired Model)",
       x = "Log2 Fold Change", y = "-Log10 Adjusted P-value")

title: W7. DEG 분석
text:
조건(예: Case vs. Control) 사이에서 발현량이 유의하게 변하는 유전자







핵심 난점: 생물학적 신호에는 항상 기술적 잡음과 개인 간 변이가 섞여 있음
최종 목표: 관측된 전체 분산에서 생물학적 신호만 뽑아내기

title: W7. DEG 분석
text:
조건(예: Case vs. Control) 사이에서 발현량이 유의하게 변하는 유전자







핵심 난점: 생물학적 신호에는 항상 기술적 잡음과 개인 간 변이가 섞여 있음
최종 목표: 관측된 전체 분산에서 생물학적 신호만 뽑아내기

title: W7. DEG 분석
text:
2. 회귀 분석 (Regression analysis)

1) 선형 회귀 (Linear regression)


















2) 분산 분해 (Variance decomposition)

“통계란 변동(variation)의 출처를 추적하는 과정이다.”

\[
Total\ Variance = \mathbf{Condition} + \mathbf{Batch} + Residual
\]

Condition (신호): 진짜 생물학적 효과
Batch (계통적 잡음): 실험 날짜, 장비, 실험자 등 통제 가능한 잡음
Residual (무작위 잡음): 피할 수 없는 확률적 오차

전략: Batch를 통계 모형에 넣어 “걷어내면” → Condition 신호가 드러남

title: W7. DEG 분석
text:
3. DESeq2의 통계 모형

1) RNA-seq 데이터의 특성

Count 자료: 0을 포함하는 이산적인 정수
과대산포 (Overdispersion): 분산 >>> 평균 → 일반적인 선형 회귀는 적절하지 않음









2) 음이항분포 (Negative Binomial Distribution)
\[
Var(\mu) = \mu + \alpha\mu^2
\]

\(\mu\): 평균 발현량 (표본 추출에서 오는 고유한 오차)
\(\alpha\mu^2\): 과대산포 (생물학적 반복 간의 변동)




3) GLM (일반화 선형 모형, Generalized Linear Model)
\[
\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1(condition) + \beta_2(batch) + \cdots
\]


















4) 산포 모수 α 추정 (Shrinkage)
표본이 작을 때(예: n=3) 유전자별 α 추정이 부정확한 문제를 보완합니다.

Gene-wise: 유전자마다 원래의 산포를 계산
Trend line: 전체 유전자에 대해 공통 추세선을 적합
Shrink: 튀는 추정값을 추세선 쪽으로 당김 → 정확도 향상, 위양성 감소









5) LFC 계산과 통계 검정

β₁(condition) = log₂FoldChange (case/control)

Control: X=0 → log(μ_control) = β₀
Case: X=1 → log(μ_case) = β₀ + β₁
∴ β₁ = log₂(μ_case / μ_control)

Wald 검정: \(z = \frac{\beta_1}{SE(\beta_1)}\) → p-value
LRT (우도비 검정, Likelihood Ratio Test): 시계열이나 3개 이상 그룹 비교에 사용 (χ² 기반)

title: W7. DEG 분석
text:
4. Design Matrix






# design 공식: 배치·교란변수를 앞에, condition을 마지막에
# design = ~ Batch + Confounding + Condition

# 기준 수준(reference level) 설정 방법
# 방법 A: 미리 지정해 두기
dds$Condition <- relevel(dds$Condition, ref = "Control")

# 방법 B: 나중에 contrast로 지정하기
results(dds, contrast = c("Condition", "Treatment", "Control"))



Design Matrix (심화)








분석 유형
임상 상황
Design Formula




짝지은 시료 (Paired)
Tumor vs. Normal, 치료 전 vs. 후
~ Patient + Treatment


상호작용항 (Interaction)
약물 반응 × 질환 아형
~ Disease + Drug + Disease:Drug


시계열 (Time-Series)
여러 시점
~ Time (LRT 사용)


임의 효과 (Random Effect)
같은 개인에서 얻은 여러 조직
DESeq2에서는 지원하지 않음 → limma-voom 사용


숨은 배치 (sva)
측정되지 않은 기술적·생물학적 요인
~ Age + Gender + SV1 + SV2 + Condition

title: W7. DEG 분석
text:
5. 실습






노트실습 데이터 내려받기



아래 파일을 R 프로젝트의 analysis/ 폴더에 저장하세요.



파일
링크




dds_filtered.rds
📥 내려받기






library(DESeq2)
library(tidyverse)

dds <- readRDS('analysis/dds_filtered.rds')

# DESeq2 실행 (짝지은 모형: ~ patient + condition)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
saveRDS(dds, file = 'analysis/dds_DESeq2.rds')

# 단순 모형 (~ condition 만)
dds@design <- as.formula('~ condition')
dds_smpl <- DESeq(dds)

# dispersion plot 확인
plotDispEsts(dds)
plotDispEsts(dds_smpl)

# 결과 추출 (contrast 지정)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "Tumor", "Normal"))







노트다중공선성 (Collinearity)



짝지은 설계(paired design)에서는 환자 ID를 모형에 넣는 순간, 나이나 성별처럼 한 환자 안에서 변하지 않는 변수는 함께 넣을 수 없습니다 (내포 구조, nested structure) → 다중공선성

title: W5. RNA-seq 데이터 전처리
text:
RNA-seq 분석의 전반적인 workflow는 다음과 같습니다 (Conesa et al., Genome Biol., 2016).

Read trimming (리드 다듬기)
Alignment (정렬)
Quantification (정량)
Normalization (정규화)
Differential analysis (차등 발현 분석)
Functional profiling (기능 분석)

text:
RNA-seq 분석의 전반적인 workflow는 다음과 같습니다 (Conesa et al., Genome Biol., 2016).

Read trimming (리드 다듬기)
Alignment (정렬)
Quantification (정량)
Normalization (정규화)
Differential analysis (차등 발현 분석)

title: W5. RNA-seq 데이터 전처리
text:
0) 품질 확인: FastQC






Per base sequence quality:
3' 말단쪽 품질을 확인
점수가 초록색 구간에 머무는지 확인
Per sequence GC content:
정규분포를 따라야 함
봉우리가 여러 개면? … 오염(contamination) 의심
Adapter Content: trimming이 필요한지 판단
Number of reads: Q20/Q30 비율 확인

title: W5. RNA-seq 데이터 전처리
text:
1) 리드 다듬기 (Read Trimming): TrimGalore





# TrimGalore의 주요 기능
# 1) 품질이 낮은 리드 제거 (Phred score Q20, 오류율 1%) - sliding window 방식
# 2) 어댑터 서열 제거 (Illumina Universal, TruSeq/Nextera)
# 3) 최소 길이 필터링 - 너무 짧은 리드는 버림

title: W5. RNA-seq 데이터 전처리
text:
2) 정렬 (Alignment): STAR

Bowtie2/BWA: DNA용; 인덱싱과 mismatch 기반
STAR: RNA-seq 전용 spliced aligner

splice junction을 인식 → 엑손에만 매핑
RAM이 많이 필요함 (>30GB)








QC 기준 (일반적으로): %Uniquely mapped reads > 80%, #mapped reads > 20M
결과 형식: SAM (텍스트) 또는 BAM (바이너리)
Galaxy: 웹 기반 전처리 도구

title: W5. RNA-seq 데이터 전처리
text:
3) 정량 (Quantification)

정렬 기반 (STAR + featureCounts)






전통적인 방식: 위치 인덱싱 → 참조 유전체에 매핑
BAM 파일이 필요하고 계산량이 많음



정렬 없이 / 유사 정렬 (Salmon, Kallisto)






리드 전체를 매핑하는 대신 짧은 k-mer (k=31) 의 일치 여부를 확인
BAM이 필요 없고 매우 빠름
여러 곳에 매핑되는 리드(multi-mapping) → EM 알고리즘으로 isoform 수준의 확률을 부여

예: read A → isoform X (0.6), isoform Y (0.4)








힌트salmon 결과(transcript)를 tximport로 불러오기




aggregation: transcript –> gene
correction: 시료별 평균 transcript 길이 (isoform switching) –> gene count 보정
import: 실수(float) –> 정수(integer)

title: W5. RNA-seq 데이터 전처리
text:
4) 필터링과 정규화

필터링 예시 (연구 설계에 따라 달라짐)

발현량이 낮은 유전자 제거: N×0.5 개 이상의 시료에서 count가 0인 유전자 제거 (N: 가장 작은 그룹의 크기)







교란 요인이 되는 유전자 제거:

미토콘드리아 (^MT-)
리보솜 (^RPS|^RPL)
면역글로불린 (^IG[HKL])





정규화가 필요한 이유

라이브러리 크기 (시퀀싱 깊이, depth): 깊이가 클수록 count가 커짐







유전자 길이: 긴 유전자일수록 count가 커짐









정규화 방법 비교









방법
보정 대상
비교 범위
비고




Raw Count
×
×
edgeR/DESeq2의 입력값


RPKM/FPKM
깊이 + 길이
시료 내
현재는 권장되지 않음


TPM
깊이 + 길이
시료 내 + 시료 간
시료별 합 = 1M


CPM
깊이
시료 간



TMM/RLE
깊이 + 조성(composition)
시료 간
DEG 분석의 표준

# 7. 시각화 ####
## 7-1. count 형태 바꾸기 (ggplot용 long 형태) ####
transform_to_long <- function(count_matrix, method_name) {
  as.data.frame(count_matrix) %>%
    rownames_to_column("Gene") %>%
    pivot_longer(-Gene, names_to = "Sample", values_to = "Count") %>%
    mutate(Method = method_name,
           # Log2 변환 (0 때문에 pseudocount +1)
           LogCount = log2(Count + 1))
}

TMM vs RLE

TMM: 기준 시료(reference sample)를 정하고 극단값을 잘라낸 뒤, housekeeping 유전자 집합을 기준으로 정규화
RLE: 각 유전자에 대해 시료 전체의 기하평균 대비 비율의 중앙값을 size factor로 사용

이 문서의 모든 예제는 아래에서 만드는 patients 데이터를 사용합니다.

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)

n <- 40

patients <- tibble(
  pt_id     = paste0("P", sprintf("%03d", 1:n)),
  gender    = sample(c("M", "F"), n, replace = TRUE),
  height    = round(rnorm(n, mean = 168, sd = 10)),
  weight    = round(rnorm(n, mean = 70,  sd = 15)),
  Age       = round(runif(n, min = 30, max = 72)),
  Diagnosis = sample(c("Diabetes", "Hypertension", "Healthy"),
                     n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.35, 0.35, 0.30)),
  disease   = Diagnosis,
  HbA1c     = round(
    case_when(
      Diagnosis == "Diabetes"     ~ rnorm(n, mean = 8.0, sd = 1.0),
      Diagnosis == "Hypertension" ~ rnorm(n, mean = 5.8, sd = 0.7),
      TRUE                        ~ rnorm(n, mean = 5.2, sd = 0.5)
    ), 1)
)

# 비교용 data.frame 버전

title: W3. 데이터 정리와 시각화
text:
2. 시각화: ggplot2
ggplot2는 세 가지 요소로 이루어집니다.

data: 데이터 프레임
aes: x축, y축, color, fill, group 등
geom: 그래프의 종류


dataframe %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = xx, y = yy)) +
  geom_function() +
  ...


미학 요소 (Aesthetics)








속성
설명
예시




color / fill
색
"red", "#RRGGBB"


linetype
선 종류
"solid", "dashed", "dotted"


size
점 / 글자 크기
mm 단위


linewidth
선 두께
mm 단위


shape
점 모양
0~25 정수


alpha
투명도
0 (투명) ~ 1 (불투명)









힌트



aes() 안에 쓰면: 변수에 자동으로 대응됩니다 → aes(color = Diagnosis)
geom_ 안에 쓰면: 고정값이 됩니다 → geom_bar(color = 'black')





① 막대 그래프 (Bar Plot): 범주형 자료의 빈도

patients %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Diagnosis)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Number of Patients by Diagnosis",
       x = "Diagnosis", y = "Count") +
  theme_classic()











② 히스토그램 (Histogram): 연속형 변수의 분포

patients %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Age Distribution", x = "Age", y = "Count") +
  theme_classic()











③ 상자 그림 (Box Plot): 그룹 간 연속형 값 비교

patients %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Diagnosis, y = HbA1c, fill = Diagnosis)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "HbA1c by Diagnosis", x = "Diagnosis", y = "HbA1c (%)") +
  theme_classic()











④ 산점도 (Scatter Plot): 두 연속형 변수의 관계

patients %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Age, y = HbA1c)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = 'darkblue') +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Age vs HbA1c", x = "Age", y = "HbA1c (%)") +
  theme_classic()











⑤ 선 그래프 (Line Plot): 시간에 따른 변화

bp_long %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = visit, y = sbp, group = pt_id, color = pt_id)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Systolic BP Across Visits",
       x = "Visit", y = "SBP (mmHg)", color = "Patient") +
  theme_classic()











그래프 꾸미기

patients %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Diagnosis, y = HbA1c, fill = Diagnosis)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "HbA1c Levels by Diagnosis",
       x = "Diagnosis", y = "HbA1c (%)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  theme_classic()











주요 테마 (Theme)



테마
설명




theme_classic()
흰 배경, 축만 표시


theme_bw()
흰 배경 + 격자선


theme_minimal()
장식을 최소화


theme_light()
밝은 톤















그래프 저장하기

# 확장자에 따라 형식이 자동으로 결정됨
ggsave("results/w3_my_result.png")

# 고해상도 TIFF (논문 투고용)
ggsave("results/w3_Figure1.tiff",
       width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 300)

# PDF (발표용; 확대해도 깨지지 않음)
ggsave("results/w3_Figure1.pdf", width = 6, height = 4)

title: W1. 생물정보학 소개
text:
Bio + information

Bio ➡️ 사람의 시료 (특정 표현형을 가진)
Information ➡️ 데이터 (오믹스, Omics)





오믹스 데이터는 NGS로 생산됩니다.
생어 염기서열 분석(Sanger Sequencing) 과 차세대 염기서열 분석(NGS) 의 차이는 무엇일까요?

Sanger sequencing … 형광 표지된 ddNTP








NGS: 라이브러리 제작(library preparation) + 합성에 의한 염기서열 분석(sequencing by synthesis)








라이브러리 제작 & 브리지 증폭(bridge amplification)




합성에 의한 염기서열 분석 (sequencing by synthesis, SBS)
   
 



NGS 라이브러리 분자: 어댑터(adapter) + 삽입체(insert)

P5/P7 (플로우셀에 결합)
Index (시료 식별자, 6–12 nt, 다중화(multiplexing)용)
Primer (예: mRNA용 PolyA, total RNA용 6-mer)




















3’ kit가 흔히 쓰이는 이유:

scRNA-seq 표준: 10x Genomics Chromium은 3’ kit를 표준으로 사용
비용 효율적이고 처리량이 높음
유전자 발현량 정량에 충분함
poly-A tail을 표적하므로 mRNA 포집 효율이 높음

5’ kit를 쓰는 경우:

TCR/BCR V(D)J 프로파일링: CDR3 영역이 5’ 말단에 위치
T 세포·B 세포 레퍼토리 연구에 필수
보통 10x Genomics 5’ kit와 V(D)J enrichment를 조합해 사용







전체론적(holistic) & 포괄적(comprehensive)
고차원 … large p, small n
다층적·계층적 구조 … 중심 원리(central dogma)




서열 정보
read 하나당 네 줄 (n = 20~30M)

@SRR21484222.626.1 626 length=51       ← Read ID
GCCTTGGTGGTGAAATGGTAGACTGGAATTCTCGGGTGCCAAGGAACTCCA  ← Sequence
+SRR21484222.626.1 626 length=51       ← Description
F:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFF:,FFFFFFFFF  ← Base call quality (Phred score)



\(Q = -10 \log_{10} P\)



Phred 점수
오류율
염기 판독 정확도




10
1 in 10
90%


20
1 in 100
99%


30
1 in 1,000
99.9%


40
1 in 10,000
99.99%










이 수업에서는 전사체(transcriptome) (RNA-seq 데이터)에 집중합니다





✅ NGS 실험 한 번 ➡️ GB에서 TB 규모의 정보 … 전통적인 실험실 방법으로는 감당할 수 없는 양
✅ 빠르게 낮아지는 NGS 비용 ➡️ 기하급수적으로 늘어나는 데이터

text:
3. R & RStudio

임상 연구자의 일반적인 작업 흐름 (?)
Excel에서 데이터 정리 → SPSS에서 분석 → 결과를 Word에 복붙 → 리뷰어 코멘트 → 처음부터 다시...






경고이 방식의 단점




데이터가 갱신되면 → 모든 표와 그림을 손으로 다시 만들어야 함
“이 p-value는 어디서 나온 거지?” → 추적하기 어려움
공동연구자와 분석 공유 → 말로 설명하거나 스크린샷






왜 R인가?
✅ Excel을 넘어서는 폭넓은 통계
✅ 무료 & 오픈소스 >> SPSS
✅ 논문 게재 수준의 시각화
✅ 생물학·의생명 패키지



1) R 설치
The Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN)








2) RStudio 설치

R용 IDE (통합 개발 환경, Integrated Development Environment)

RStudio Desktop - Posit

NES, FDR (q-value)







library(GEOquery)
library(TCGAbiolinks)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(tidyverse)

# Option 1: Download directly from GEO
# gse <- getGEO("GSE****", GSEMatrix = TRUE)

# Option 2: TCGA (web browser recommended for large datasets)
# query <- GDCquery(project = "TCGA-LUAD", ...)
# GDCdownload(query)
# data <- GDCprepare(query)

# Load pre-saved files
countData <- readRDS('examples/data/w6_raw_counts_final.rds')
colData   <- readRDS('examples/data/w6_meta_data_final.rds')

cat("Count matrix:", nrow(countData), "genes x", ncol(countData), "samples\n")
cat("Sample groups:\n"); print(table(colData$tissue_type))







NoteStudy Design Checklist



✅ N > 30 per group: ensures adequate statistical power
✅ Clear phenotype: binary comparison (Tumor vs. Normal, Responder vs. Non-responder)
✅ Potential batch effects: samples from different institutions or time points?
✅ Confounding variables: age, sex, smoking history, treatment history







library(DESeq2)

# Set factor levels — control group must be the reference!
colData$condition <- factor(
  colData$tissue_type,
  levels = c("Normal", "Tumor")  # Normal is the reference
)

# Build DESeq2 dataset with design matrix
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = countData,
  colData   = colData,
  design    = ~ patient + condition  # account for paired patient structure
)






# Method 1: Simple threshold (remove total count < 10)
keep_simple <- rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10

# Method 2: Group-size-aware filtering (recommended)
# Keep genes with at least 1 count in >= 50% of the smallest group
smallest_group <- min(table(colData$condition))
keep_group     <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 1) >= (smallest_group * 0.5)

cat("Removed (simple):     ", sum(!keep_simple), "genes\n")
cat("Removed (group-aware):", sum(!keep_group),  "genes\n")

dds_filtered <- dds[keep_group, ]

# Remove confounding gene categories
all_genes  <- rownames(dds_filtered)
mt_genes   <- grep("^MT-",      all_genes, value = TRUE)  # mitochondrial
ribo_genes <- grep("^RPS|^RPL", all_genes, value = TRUE)  # ribosomal
ig_genes   <- grep("^IG[HKL]",  all_genes, value = TRUE)  # immunoglobulin

cat("Contaminating genes to remove:", length(c(mt_genes, ribo_genes, ig_genes)), "\n")

contam       <- c(mt_genes, ribo_genes, ig_genes)
dds_filtered <- dds_filtered[!(all_genes %in% contam), ]

saveRDS(dds_filtered, 'examples/analysis/w6_dds_filtered.rds')






# Variance Stabilizing Transformation for visualization
vsd <- vst(dds_filtered, blind = FALSE)

# PCA Plot: check for batch effects and outliers
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "condition") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "PCA Plot: Sample Quality Check")







WarningWhat to Look for in the PCA Plot




PC1 separates conditions? → Strong biological signal, good to proceed
Obvious outliers? → Consider excluding and re-running
No clear grouping? → Suspect batch effects; apply limma::removeBatchEffect()








dds <- readRDS('examples/analysis/w6_dds_filtered.rds')

# Run DESeq2 (dispersion estimation → GLM fitting → Wald test)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
saveRDS(dds, 'examples/analysis/w7_dds_DESeq2.rds')

# Extract results (Tumor vs. Normal)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "Tumor", "Normal"))
summary(res)

# LFC Shrinkage: stabilize effect size estimates for low-count genes
library(apeglm)
resLFC <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "condition_Tumor_vs_Normal", type = "apeglm")
saveRDS(resLFC, 'examples/analysis/w9_res_DESeq2_lfcShrink.rds')






library(ggrepel)
library(pheatmap)

resLFC <- readRDS('examples/analysis/w9_res_DESeq2_lfcShrink.rds')

res_df <- as.data.frame(resLFC) %>%
  rownames_to_column("gene_id")

# ---- Volcano Plot ----
p_thr   <- 0.05
lfc_thr <- 1

vol_data <- res_df %>%
  mutate(diffexpressed = case_when(
    log2FoldChange >  lfc_thr & padj < p_thr ~ "UP",
    log2FoldChange < -lfc_thr & padj < p_thr ~ "DOWN",
    TRUE ~ "NO"
  ))

ggplot(vol_data, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = diffexpressed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("DOWN" = "blue", "NO" = "grey", "UP" = "red")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-lfc_thr, lfc_thr), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(p_thr), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = head(arrange(vol_data, padj), 10),
    aes(label = gene_id), color = "black"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Volcano Plot",
       x     = "Log2 Fold Change",
       y     = "-Log10 Adjusted P-value")


# ---- Heatmap of Top 20 DEGs ----
vsd <- readRDS('examples/analysis/w6_dds_vsd.rds')

top_genes <- res_df %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(log2FoldChange))) %>%
  head(20) %>%
  .$gene_id

mat <- assay(vsd)[top_genes, ]

# Sample annotation sidebar
anno_col <- as.data.frame(colData(dds)[, c("gender", "condition")])

pheatmap(
  mat,
  scale          = "row",   # z-score normalization across samples
  show_rownames  = TRUE,
  show_colnames  = FALSE,
  annotation_col = anno_col,
  cluster_cols   = TRUE,
  main           = "Top 20 DEGs Heatmap"
)

# gseGO() → dotplot() → gseaplot2() → cnetplot()

title: W9. Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)
text:
1. Introduction: Gene sets

after DEG analysis…
From the last week, we identified ~5,500 DEGs (Tumor vs. Normal) with FDR≤0.05 & |LFC|≥1 … So What? “Do they functionally cluster in specific biological processes?“





Before running ORA, you need to understand the databases that link genes to biological pathways



Major Databases of gene sets



Database
Characteristics
Typical Use Case




KEGG
Metabolic and disease pathways
Metabolic disease, signaling cascades


Gene Ontology(GO)
Hierarchical gene function classification
Most widely used across all fields


Reactome
Peer-reviewed, manually curated pathways
Detailed biochemical mechanisms


MSigDB / Enrichr
225+ diverse gene set collections
Exploratory analyses











Three GO Categories

BP (Biological Process): What is the gene doing? (e.g., Cell division, Inflammation) … Most used in clinical research
MF (Molecular Function): What is the molecular activity? (e.g., Kinase activity, ATP binding)
CC (Cellular Component): Where is it located? (e.g., Nucleus, Membrane)

title: W9. Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)
text:
2. Statistical Principle: Fisher’s Exact Test

Intuition: The Urn Problem

Q: Does my DEG list contain more genes from the “Inflammation” pathway than expected by chance?








2×2 Contingency Table










In Pathway (Red)
Not in Pathway (White)
Total




DEGs (drawn)
100 (a, hit)
400 (b)
500


Non-DEGs
900 (c)
18,600 (d)
19,500


Total
1,000
19,000
20,000 (N)





Two Effect Size Metrics
Odds Ratio (OR): \[OR = \frac{a/c}{b/d} = \frac{a \times d}{b \times c} = \frac{100 \times 18{,}600}{400 \times 900} \approx 5.2\]
Fold Enrichment (FE) — more intuitive and conservative: \[FE = \frac{a/(a+c)}{(a+b)/N} = \frac{\text{% of pathway genes among DEGs}}{\text{% of pathway genes in background}}\]






ImportantOR vs. FE — Which to Use?




OR: Compares the two groups (selected vs. not selected); can overestimate effect size with small DEG lists
FE: How much more enriched relative to the background; more commonly reported in papers
In practice: Report both, but the p-value (hypergeometric test) and FDR-corrected p-value are the critical outputs






P-value: Hypergeometric Distribution




In Pathway (Red)
Not in Pathway (White)
Total




DEGs (drawn)
100 (k)
400 (n-k)
500 (n)


Non-DEGs
900 (K-k)
18,600 (N-n -K-k)
19,500 (N-n)


Total
1,000 (K)
19,000 (N-K)
20,000 (N)




\(N\): total number of genes (background)
\(K\): number of genes in the pathway
\(n\): number of DEGs
\(k\): number of DEGs that hit the pathway

\[P(X = k) = \frac{\binom{K}{k}\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}\]
\[\text{p-value} = \sum_{i=k}^{\min(n,K)} P(X=i) \quad \text{(one-tailed test)}\]






WarningThe Importance of Background Genes



Suppose you tested a cancer gene panel (n = 500) and found 50 DEGs.
Running ORA without a proper background → results will be trivially enriched in cancer pathways (selection bias!).
Correct approach: Use all genes that were actually tested by DESeq2 (i.e., genes where padj is not NA) as the background universe.

title: W9. Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)
text:
Practice: Enrichr

Data Preparation in R

library(DESeq2)
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Load LFC-shrunken results
resLFC <- readRDS('examples/data/w9_res_DESeq2_lfcShrink.rds')
res_df <- resLFC %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(gene_id = rownames(.)) %>%
  arrange(padj)

# 2. Extract DEG list (|LFC| >= 1 & FDR <= 0.05)
genes <- res_df %>%
  filter(abs(log2FoldChange) >= 1, padj <= 0.05) %>%
  .$gene_id

cat("Number of DEGs:", length(genes), "\n")

# 3. Save to file (for Enrichr upload)
write.table(genes,
            file      = 'examples/analysis/w9_myDEGs.txt',
            sep       = "\t",
            quote     = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE,
            col.names = FALSE)

# 4. Save background gene list
total <- res_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(padj)) %>%
  .$gene_id

write.table(total,
            file      = 'examples/analysis/w9_myDEGs.txt',
            sep       = "\t",
            quote     = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE,
            col.names = FALSE)

cat("Number of background genes:", length(total), "\n")




How to Use Enrichr

Go to https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/
Paste your DEG list (myDEGs.txt)
Upload your background gene list (total.txt)

Pathways tab → explore Reactome, KEGG
Ontologies tab → explore GO Biological Process








TipInterpreting Enrichr Results




Combined Score = log(p-value) × z-score (Enrichr-specific metric)
Only pathways passing Adjusted P-value ≤ 0.05 are considered significant
Pathways that appear consistently across multiple databases carry higher confidence

title: W10. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)
text:
ORA Limitation
Explanation




Cutoff dependency
Genes with padj=1e-10 and padj=0.049 are treated identically


Direction ignored
Information about up- vs. down-regulation is discarded


Boundary problem
If all genes in an important pathway have padj=0.06, ORA misses it entirely



✅ Solution: GSEA

Uses all genes, ranked by a continuous metric
No cutoff required → no information loss
Preserves directionality of expression change

title: W10. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)
text:
2. The GSEA Algorithm

1) Input: Ranked Gene List





Ranking metric options:








Metric
Formula
Characteristics




log2FoldChange
Used directly
Simple; focuses on effect size


Wald Statistic (recommended)
DESeq2 stat column
Integrates LFC + uncertainty


Pi-value
\(-\log_{10}(p) \times \text{sign}(LFC)\)
Emphasizes statistical significance









TipWhich Ranking Metric Should I Use?



All three metrics are highly correlated (r > 0.9), but in general:

Wald statistic: Accounts for both effect size and its standard error → most balanced choice
Pi-value: Emphasizes genes with strong statistical support
Best practice: run all three and compare (sensitivity analysis)






2) Enrichment Score (ES) Calculation
A running sum is calculated for each gene set as you walk through the ranked list:

Walk through all genes from rank 1 to N:
  → Hit a gene IN the pathway:  running sum += 1/K  (K = pathway size)
  → Hit a gene NOT in pathway:  running sum -= 1/(N-K)

ES = maximum deviation of the running sum from zero (KS statistic)
Patterns of ES:





Up-regulated pathway:   ^^^^^^^\_____  → peak near the top
Random (not enriched):  ~/\/\/\/\/\/\  → fluctuates around zero
Down-regulated pathway: _______/^^^^^  → peak near the bottom



3) Statistical Significance: Permutation Test





1. Calculate ES from the actual data
          ↓
2. Randomly shuffle sample labels 1,000 times
          ↓
3. Generate 1,000 random ES values → build null distribution
          ↓
4. Where does the observed ES fall relative to the null?
NES (Normalized Enrichment Score): \[NES = \frac{ES_{observed}}{\text{mean}(ES_{random})}\] Corrects for pathway size differences → enables fair comparison across pathways
FDR (q-value): \[\text{FDR} = \frac{N_{>NES\text{ in random}}}{N_{>NES\text{ in observed}}}\]

title: W10. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)
text:
3. Practice: clusterProfiler

⓪ set-up

Package Installation

if (!require("clusterProfiler")) BiocManager::install("clusterProfiler")
if (!require("msigdbr"))         BiocManager::install("msigdbr")
if (!require("enrichplot"))      BiocManager::install("enrichplot")
if (!require("ReactomePA"))      BiocManager::install("ReactomePA")
if (!require("org.Hs.eg.db"))    BiocManager::install("org.Hs.eg.db")



gene ID conversion (if needed): org.Hs.eg.db + mapIds()






NoteUnderstanding Gene ID Systems












ID Type
Example
Source
Use Case




Gene Symbol
TP53, EGFR
HGNC
Human-readable (may have duplicates)


Ensembl ID
ENSG00000141510
EBI
RNA-seq aligner output; unique and stable


Entrez ID
7157
NCBI
Gene set labels (KEGG, GO)



For GSEA, you typically need to convert Gene Symbols or Ensembl IDs to Entrez IDs.



library(tidyverse)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
library(AnnotationDbi)

# Load DESeq2 results
res        <- readRDS('examples/data/w7_res_DESeq2.rds')
res_df <- as.data.frame(res) %>%
  filter(!is.na(pvalue) & !is.na(log2FoldChange)) %>%
  mutate(gene = rownames(.))

# Example: Gene Symbol → Entrez ID
my_ids <- res_df$gene  # vector of Gene Symbols

my_entrez <- mapIds(
  org.Hs.eg.db,
  keys      = my_ids,
  column    = "ENTREZID",  # desired output ID type
  keytype   = "SYMBOL",    # input ID type
  multiVals = "first"      # handle 1-to-many mappings: keep first
)

# Combine into a data frame for inspection
my_genes <- tibble(
  gene   = my_ids,
  entrez = my_entrez
)
head(my_genes)

# check for NAs (novel genes, pseudogenes, version mismatches, etc.)
sum(is.na(my_genes$entrez))
my_genes %>% filter(is.na(entrez))





① Data Loading

library(clusterProfiler)
library(enrichplot)
library(msigdbr)

# 1. Load DESeq2 results
res_shrink <- readRDS('examples/data/w9_res_DESeq2_lfcShrink.rds')
res        <- readRDS('examples/data/w7_res_DESeq2.rds')  # needed for stat column

# 2. Convert to data frame and remove NAs
res_df <- as.data.frame(res) %>%
  filter(!is.na(pvalue) & !is.na(log2FoldChange)) %>%
  mutate(gene = rownames(.))

# 3. Add Entrez ID
res_df <- res_df %>% left_join(my_genes, by = "gene")

# 4. Compute ranking metrics
res_df$rank_lfc  <- res_shrink$log2FoldChange
res_df$rank_pi   <- -log10(res_df$pvalue) * sign(res_df$log2FoldChange)
res_df$rank_wald <- res_df$stat

# Check correlation between metrics
cat("LFC vs Pi-value:", round(cor(res_df$rank_lfc, res_df$rank_pi,  use = "complete"), 3), "\n")
cat("LFC vs Wald:    ", round(cor(res_df$rank_lfc, res_df$rank_wald, use = "complete"), 3), "\n")
cat("Pi  vs Wald:    ", round(cor(res_df$rank_pi,  res_df$rank_wald, use = "complete"), 3), "\n")

# 5. Remove duplicate Entrez IDs and drop NAs
res_df <- res_df %>%
  distinct(entrez, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(entrez))

# 6. Build the final ranked gene list (using Wald statistic)
geneList        <- res_df$rank_wald
names(geneList) <- res_df$gene   # use when keyType = "SYMBOL"
geneList        <- sort(geneList, decreasing = TRUE)

cat("\nTop 5 (up-regulated):\n");   print(head(geneList, 5))
cat("\nBottom 5 (down-regulated):\n"); print(tail(geneList, 5))




② Running GSEA

# ---- (1) GO Biological Process ----
gsea_go <- gseGO(
  geneList     = geneList,
  OrgDb        = org.Hs.eg.db,
  keyType      = "SYMBOL",
  ont          = "BP",         # choose from: BP, MF, CC
  minGSSize    = 10,           # exclude very small pathways
  maxGSSize    = 500,          # exclude very broad, non-specific pathways
  pvalueCutoff = 1,            # keep all results for now; filter later
  by           = "fgsea"       # fast approximation method
)
saveRDS(gsea_go, 'examples/analysis/w10_gsea_GO.rds')



# ---- (2) Reactome ----
library(ReactomePA)

# Note: Reactome requires Entrez IDs!
geneList_entrez        <- res_df$rank_wald
names(geneList_entrez) <- res_df$entrez
geneList_entrez        <- sort(geneList_entrez, decreasing = TRUE)

gsea_reactome <- gsePathway(
  geneList     = geneList_entrez,
  pvalueCutoff = 1
)
saveRDS(gsea_reactome, 'examples/analysis/w10_gsea_reactome.rds')


# ---- (3) MSigDB Hallmark Gene Sets ----
# Hallmark: 50 well-defined biological states — good for first pass
msig_h <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", category = "H") %>%
  transmute(gs_name, ncbi_gene)

gsea_hallmark <- GSEA(
  geneList,
  TERM2GENE      = msig_h,
  pvalueCutoff   = 1,
  pAdjustMethod  = "BH",
  minGSSize      = 10,
  maxGSSize      = 500,
  by             = "fgsea"
)
saveRDS(gsea_hallmark, 'examples/analysis/w10_gsea_hallmarks.rds')

Category
Code
Description

50 coherent biological states — best starting point


Curated

KEGG, Reactome, WikiPathways

⑤ Visualization

library(ggplot2)
library(ggridges)

gsea_res <- readRDS('examples/analysis/w10_gsea_GO.rds')

# ---- (1) Dot Plot: overview of enriched pathways ----
# x = NES, dot size = gene count, color = adjusted p-value
dotplot(gsea_res, showCategory = 5, split = ".sign") +
  ggtitle("GO BP Enrichment")

# Split by up- and down-regulated pathways
dotplot(gsea_res, showCategory = 5, split = ".sign") +
  facet_grid(. ~ .sign) +
  ggtitle("GO BP Enrichment (Activated vs. Suppressed)")


# ---- (2) Classic GSEA Enrichment Plot ----
p1 <- gseaplot2(
  gsea_res,
  geneSetID = 1,
  title     = gsea_res$Description[1]
)
print(p1)

# Show top 3 pathways together
p2 <- gseaplot2(gsea_res, geneSetID = 1:3)
print(p2)


# ---- (3) Ridge Plot: distribution of ranked metric ----
ridgeplot(gsea_res, showCategory = 5) +
  labs(x     = "Enrichment Distribution",
       title = "Gene expression distribution across pathways")


# ---- (4) Network Plot: gene–pathway connections ----
cnetplot(gsea_res, foldChange = geneList)




⑥ Saving Results and Extracting Core Enrichment Genes

# Save full results as CSV
gsea_df <- as.data.frame(gsea_res)
write.csv(gsea_df, "examples/analysis/w10_GSEA_Results.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Inspect the top pathway
top_pathway <- gsea_df[1, ]
cat("Top pathway: ", top_pathway$Description, "\n")
cat("NES:         ", round(top_pathway$NES, 3), "\n")
cat("FDR:         ", round(top_pathway$p.adjust, 4), "\n")

# Extract core enrichment genes (the "leading edge")
core_genes <- strsplit(top_pathway$core_enrichment, "/")[[1]]
cat("\nCore enrichment genes (top 10):\n")
print(head(core_genes, 10))

title: W10. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)
text:
4. Summary

ORA vs. GSEA Comparison








Feature
ORA
GSEA




Input
DEG list + background
All genes, ranked


Cutoff required
Yes (binary)
No (continuous)


Statistical test
Hypergeometric / Fisher’s Exact
Permutation test (KS statistic)


Effect direction
Ignored
Preserved (up vs. down)


Effect size metric
Odds Ratio, Fold Enrichment
NES (Normalized Enrichment Score)


Advantage
Intuitive, fast
No information loss, direction-aware


Disadvantage
Cutoff-sensitive, loses information
Computationally intensive, harder to interpret


Best used when
Clear, well-defined DEG list exists
Exploratory analysis, detecting subtle changes









Caution❌ Pitfalls or common mistakes to avoid




No background gene set (ORA): Always use the actually-tested genes, not the whole genome
Duplicate Entrez IDs: Use distinct(entrez, .keep_all = TRUE) to deduplicate
Not removing NAs: Filter out NA pvalue/log2FoldChange before building the ranked list
Cutoff shopping: Adjusting thresholds until you get the desired result = p-hacking
Ignoring gene set size: Set minGSSize = 10 and maxGSSize = 500 to exclude trivial pathways
Reporting NES without FDR: Always check FDR (q-value) ≤ 0.25 (GSEA standard) or ≤ 0.05 (conservative)

title: W10. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)

📝 Week 10 Assignment
1. Threshold Effect in ORA
Run enrichGO(BP) twice using different gene lists from the same DESeq2 results:

List A (Strict): padj < 0.01 & |log2FC| > 2
List B (Lenient): padj < 0.05 & |log2FC| > 0.5


library(clusterProfiler)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)

# List A — Strict
genes_A <- res_df %>%
  filter(padj < 0.01, abs(log2FoldChange) > 2) %>%
  .$gene

ora_A <- enrichGO(
  gene         = genes_A,
  universe     = total_genes,   # always set background!
  OrgDb        = org.Hs.eg.db,
  keyType      = "SYMBOL",
  ont          = "BP",
  pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
  qvalueCutoff = 0.2
)

# List B — Lenient
genes_B <- res_df %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05, abs(log2FoldChange) > 0.5) %>%
  .$gene

ora_B <- enrichGO(
  gene         = genes_B,
  universe     = total_genes,
  OrgDb        = org.Hs.eg.db,
  keyType      = "SYMBOL",
  ont          = "BP",
  pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
  qvalueCutoff = 0.2
)

dotplot(ora_A, showCategory = 5) + ggtitle("Strict (List A)")
dotplot(ora_B, showCategory = 5) + ggtitle("Lenient (List B)")

title: W6. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Visualize data before statistical analysis to understand its overall characteristics and quality

Quality Control: identify outlier samples
Batch Effect Detection: check whether technical noise (experiment date, instrument, etc.) is masking biological signal
Heteroscedasticity: variance increases with expression level → a small number of highly expressed genes can dominate the entire analysis




we need to transform our data (RNA-seq data) for statistic analyses











Caution



vst/rlog transformed values are for visualization only; raw counts must be used for differential analysis!









Suitable for n ≥ 30 (large sample sizes)
Based on a global trend → fast
asinh transformation for highly-expressed genes
















Suitable for n < 30 (small sample sizes)
Per-gene shrinkage (Bayesian estimation) → slow
Suppresses noise in low-count genes













NoteImagine this



gene A (low):
sample 1: 1, sample 2: 5 ➡️ logFC = log2(5/1) = 2.32 … noise ↑

gene B (high):
sample 1: 1000, sample 2: 1004 ➡️ logFC = log2(1004/1000) = 0.005 … noise ↓ (stabilized)

title: W6. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
2. Visual Exploration (QC Part II)
What to check through visualization:

Is there a difference between groups?
Are there any outlier samples?
Is there a batch effect?







Notedownload practice data



save the following files in data/ in your R project



File
Link




raw_counts_final.rds
📥 Download


meta_data_final.rds
📥 Download







data transformation for visualization

# 1. read data (count table and metadata) ####
countData <- readRDS('data/raw_counts_final.rds')
dim(countData)
head(countData[,1:5])

colData <- readRDS("data/meta_data_final.rds")
head(colData)
table(colData$tissue_type)

# check sample ids of the count table and metadata
all(colnames(countData) == colData$barcode) # should be TRUE

# set the Factor level (condition)
# default: alphabetical ... ref = Control/Normal
colData$condition <- factor(colData$tissue_type, levels = c("Normal", "Tumor")) 
colData$condition
# case / control ... treatment / control ... KO / control


# 2. DESeq2 object (dds) ####
# countData, colData, design
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = countData,
                              colData = colData,
                              design = ~ patient + condition) # DEG by condition
colData$patient = gsub('-','_',colData$patient)
dds

# 3. Pre-filtering (de-noising) ####
dim(counts(dds))

head(counts(dds)[,1:4])
head(counts(dds)[,1:4]>=1)
head(rowSums(counts(dds)[,1:4]>=1))
head(rowSums(counts(dds)>=1))
rowSums(counts(dds)) %>% head

## 3-1. lowly expressed genes (for speed-up & statistical power) ####
### option 1: simple (Total Count < 10?) ####
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10
head(keep)
cat(paste("   Removed", sum(!keep), "low count genes.\n"))
cat(paste("   Remaining genes:", sum(keep), "\n"))
dds_filtered <- dds[keep, ]

### option 2: considring group size (recommended) ####
# Total Count < 10 in the smallest group?
# ex: Control(3), Case(10) -> non-zero counts in at least 3 samples?
main_condition = 'condition'
smallestGroupSize <- min(table(colData[[main_condition]]))
smallestGroupSize*0.4
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 1) >= (smallestGroupSize*0.5)
cat(paste("   Removed", sum(!keep), "low count genes.\n"))
cat(paste("   Remaining genes:", sum(keep), "\n"))
dds_filtered <- dds[keep, ]

## 3-2. confounding genes ####
all_genes <- rownames(dds_filtered)
head(all_genes)
# Mitochodiral: starting with "^MT-" 
mt_genes <- grep("^MT-", all_genes, value = TRUE)
mt_genes
# Ribosomal: starting with "^RPS|^RPL"
ribo_genes <- grep("^RPS|^RPL", all_genes, value = TRUE)
ribo_genes
# Immunoglobulin: starting with "^IG[HKL]" : "IGH", "IGK", "IGL"
ig_genes <- grep("^IG[HKL]", all_genes, value = TRUE)
ig_genes
# filtering gene list
contam_list <- c(mt_genes, ribo_genes, ig_genes)
length(contam_list)
# !: 'NOT'
keep_indices <- !(all_genes %in% contam_list)
dds_filtered <- dds_filtered[keep_indices, ]
dds_filtered
saveRDS(dds_filtered, 'dds_filtered.rds')

# 4. Variance Stabilizing Transformation (vst) ####
## 4-1. vst (normalization and transformation) ####
vsd <- vst(dds_filtered, blind=FALSE) 
# blind = FALSE: using design (recommended), blind=TRUE: using only technical noises

# check the result visually
vsd_data = assay(vsd)




Sample Correlation Heatmap

library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)

sampleDists <- dist(t(vsd_data))
sampleDistMatrix <- as.matrix(sampleDists)
rownames(sampleDistMatrix) <- paste(vsd$condition, vsd$type, sep = "-")
colnames(sampleDistMatrix) <- NULL

colors <- colorRampPalette(rev(brewer.pal(9, "Blues")))(255)
pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix,
         clustering_distance_rows = sampleDists,
         clustering_distance_cols = sampleDists,
         col = colors)









PCA Plot

# PCA
pca_res <- prcomp(t(vsd_data))
pca_coords <- as.data.frame(pca_res$x[, 1:2])

ggplot(pca_coords, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggtitle("PCA Result") +
  theme_bw()









PCA vs. MDS














PCA
MDS




Input
Raw data matrix (sample × gene)
Distance matrix (sample × sample)


Goal
Preserve variance
Preserve pairwise distances


Method
Eigen decomposition
Coordinate reconstruction


Benefit
Loadings reveal important genes
Supports various distance metrics
(Euclidean-PCA, Correlation, Bray-Curtis)


Use
General QC, sample clustering
Microbiome, non-Euclidean distance

title: W6. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
3. Batch Effect

Technical noise arising from experiment date, sequencing platform, operator, etc.
Inspect alongside batch metadata in the PCA plot
Correction strategies:

For visualization: use residuals from limma::removeBatchEffect()
For statistical testing: include batch in the design matrix (covered next week)



library(limma)

mat <- assay(vsd)
mm <- model.matrix(~condition, colData(vsd))
mat2 <- removeBatchEffect(mat, batch = vsd$patient, design = mm)

# PCA after batch removal
rv <- rowVars(mat2)
select <- order(rv, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(min(500, length(rv)))]
pca <- prcomp(t(mat2[select, ]))
percentVar <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2))

pcaData2 <- data.frame(PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2],
                        condition = colData(vsd)$condition)

ggplot(pcaData2, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  xlab(paste0("PC1: ", percentVar[1], "% variance")) +
  ylab(paste0("PC2: ", percentVar[2], "% variance")) +
  ggtitle("PCA - After Patient Effect Removal") +
  theme_bw()

title: W4. Public Database Exploration
text:
Tips: Gene ID Conversion
Common gene ID systems used in RNA-seq data:









ID Type
Example
Source
Use Case




Gene Symbol
TP53, EGFR
HGNC
Human-readable (may have duplicates)


Ensembl ID
ENSG00000141510
EBI
RNA-seq aligner output; unique and stable


Entrez ID
7157
NCBI
Gene set labels (KEGG, GO)




Conversion Method: org.Hs.eg.db + mapIds()

library(tidyverse)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
library(AnnotationDbi)

# remove version numbers from Ensembl IDs
my_ids <- rownames(count_matrix)
head(my_ids)  # ENSG00000141510.15

my_ids <- sapply(my_ids, function(x) {
  strsplit(x, '\\.') %>% unlist %>% .[[1]]
})
my_ids <- as.character(my_ids)

# Ensembl → Symbol
my_symbol <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
                    keys = my_ids,
                    column = "SYMBOL",
                    keytype = "ENSEMBL",
                    multiVals = "first")

# Ensembl → Entrez ID (for GSEA/KEGG)
my_entrez <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
                    keys = my_ids,
                    column = "ENTREZID",
                    keytype = "ENSEMBL",
                    multiVals = "first")

# inspect
my_genes <- tibble(ids = my_ids,
                   symbol = my_symbol,
                   entrez = my_entrez)

# check for NAs (novel genes, pseudogenes, version mismatches, etc.)
sum(is.na(my_genes$symbol))
my_genes %>% filter(is.na(symbol))

title: W1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
text:
Bio + information

Bio ➡️ Human samples (with certain phenotypes)
Information ➡️ Data (Omics)





Omics data is generated by NGS
What is difference between Sanger Sequencing and Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)?

Sanger sequencing … ddNTP with flourchromes








NGS: library preparation + sequencing by synthesis








Library prep & bridge amplification




sequencing by synthesis (SBS)
   
 



NGS library molecule: adapter + insert

P5/P7 (binding to flow cell)
Index (Sample identifier, 6-12nt, multiplexing)
Primer (e.g., PolyA for mRNA, 6-mer for total RNAs)




















Why 3’ is commonly used:

scRNA-seq standard: 10x Genomics Chromium uses the 3’ kit as the standard
Cost-effective and high throughput
Sufficient for quantifying gene expression levels

title: W3. Data Wrangling & Visualization
text:
2. Visualization: ggplot2
ggplot2 is built on three components:

data: a data frame
aes: x-axis, y-axis, color, fill, group, etc.
geom: the type of plot


dataframe %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = xx, y = yy)) +
  geom_function() +
  ...


Aesthetics








Property
Description
Example




color / fill
Color
"red", "#RRGGBB"


linetype
Line type
"solid", "dashed", "dotted"


size
Point / text size
in mm


linewidth
Line width
in mm


shape
Point shape
integer 0–25


alpha
Transparency
0 (transparent) – 1 (opaque)









Tip



Inside aes(): maps to a variable automatically → aes(color = Diagnosis)
Inside geom_: fixed value → geom_bar(color = 'black')





① Bar Plot: frequency of categorical data

patients %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Diagnosis)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Number of Patients by Diagnosis",
       x = "Diagnosis", y = "Count") +
  theme_classic()











② Histogram: distribution of a continuous variable

patients %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Age Distribution", x = "Age", y = "Count") +
  theme_classic()

title: W5. Pre-processing
text:
0) Quality Check: FastQC






Per base sequence quality:
check quality toward the 3' end
verify that scores remain in the green zone
Per sequence GC content:
should follow a normal distribution
multiple peaks? … contamination
Adapter Content: determines whether trimming is necessary
Number of reads: check Q20/Q30 ratios

title: W5. Pre-processing
text:
1) Read Trimming: TrimGalore





# TrimGalore key functions
# 1) Remove low quality reads (Phred score Q20, error rate 1%) - sliding window
# 2) Remove adapter sequences (Illumina Universal, TruSeq/Nextera)
# 3) Minimum length filtering - discard reads that are too short

title: W5. Pre-processing
text:
2) Alignment: STAR

Bowtie2/BWA: for DNA; indexing & mismatch-based
STAR: spliced aligner dedicated to RNA-seq

Recognizes splice junctions → maps to exons only
Requires high RAM (>30GB)








QC criterion (general): %Uniquely mapped reads > 80%, #mapped reads > 20M
Output format: SAM (text) or BAM (binary)
Galaxy: web-based tool for pre-processing

title: W5. Pre-processing
text:
3) Quantification

Alignment-based (STAR + featureCounts)






Traditional approach: position indexing → mapping to reference
Requires BAM files; computationally intensive



Alignment-free / Pseudo-alignment (Salmon, Kallisto)






Uses short k-mer (k=31) compatibility checks instead of full read mapping
No BAM required; very fast
Multi-mapping reads → isoform-level probabilities assigned via EM algorithm

e.g., read A → isoform X (0.6), isoform Y (0.4)








Tiptximport using salmon outputs (transcripts)




aggregation: transcripts –> gene
correction: average transcript length per sample (isoform switching) –> gene count correction
import: float number –> integer

title: W5. Pre-processing
text:
4) Filtering and Normalization

Filtering examples (depending on your study)

Remove low-count genes: remove genes with zero counts in ≥ N×0.5 samples (N: the smallest group)







Remove confounding genes:

Mitochondrial (^MT-)
Ribosomal (^RPS|^RPL)
Immunoglobulin (^IG[HKL])





Why Normalization is Needed

Library size (depth): higher sequencing depth → higher counts







Gene length: longer genes → higher counts

title: W7. DEG Analysis
text:
2. Regression analysis

1) Linear regression


















2) Variance decomposition

“Statistics is the process of tracing the source of variation.”

\[
Total\ Variance = \mathbf{Condition} + \mathbf{Batch} + Residual
\]

Condition (Signal): the true biological effect
Batch (systematic noise): controllable noise from experiment date, instrument, operator, etc.
Residual (random noise): unavoidable stochastic error

Strategy: include Batch in the statistical model to “regress it out” → the Condition signal is revealed

title: W7. DEG Analysis
text:
3. Statistical Model of DESeq2

1) Characteristics of RNA-seq Data

Count data: discrete integers including zero
Overdispersion: variance >>> mean → standard linear regression is not appropriate









2) Negative Binomial Distribution
\[
Var(\mu) = \mu + \alpha\mu^2
\]

\(\mu\): mean expression (intrinsic sampling error)
\(\alpha\mu^2\): overdispersion (variation across biological replicates)




3) GLM (Generalized Linear Model)
\[
\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1(condition) + \beta_2(batch) + \cdots
\]


















4) Estimating Dispersion α (Shrinkage)
Addresses inaccurate per-gene α estimation in small samples (e.g., n=3):

Gene-wise: calculate the raw dispersion for each gene
Trend line: fit a global trend line across all genes
Shrink: pull noisy estimates toward the trend line → improved accuracy, reduced false positives









5) LFC Calculation and Statistical Testing

β₁(condition) = log₂FoldChange (case/control)

Control: X=0 → log(μ_control) = β₀
Case: X=1 → log(μ_case) = β₀ + β₁
∴ β₁ = log₂(μ_case / μ_control)

Wald Test: \(z = \frac{\beta_1}{SE(\beta_1)}\) → p-value
LRT (Likelihood Ratio Test): used for time-series or ≥3 group comparisons (χ²-based)

res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "Tumor", "Normal"))







NoteCollinearity



In a paired design, once patient ID is included in the model, variables such as age or gender cannot be added because they do not vary within a patient (nested structure) → collinearity

title: W8. DEG Results Processing
text:
p-value: the probability of observing the result by chance under the null hypothesis (H₀: no difference between groups)
Multiple testing problem: testing 10,000 genes at p < 0.05 would yield ~500 spuriously significant results → dramatic increase in false positives





Bonferroni: \(\alpha / n_{total}\) → too conservative
FDR (False Discovery Rate): \(FDR = \frac{FP}{FP + TP}\)










“Stricter for higher ranks, more lenient for lower ranks”

\[
FDR \leq \frac{n_{total} \cdot p_{cut}}{i} \leq \alpha(0.05)
\]
\[
p_{cut} \leq \frac{i}{n_{total}} \cdot \alpha
\]

adjusted p-value (padj) … (with cumulative minimum applied) \[
p \times \frac{n_{total}}{i}
\]


##| eval: true
 
## Manual implementation of the BH procedure
pvalues <- c(0.04, 0.001, 0.05, 0.0001, 0.2)
genes <- c("GeneA", "GeneB", "GeneC", "GeneD", "GeneE")
df <- data.frame(Gene = genes, P_raw = pvalues)
df <- df[order(df$P_raw), ]
m <- nrow(df)
alpha <- 0.05
df$Rank <- 1:m
df$BH_Threshold <- (df$Rank / m) * alpha
df$Pass <- df$P_raw <= df$BH_Threshold
df$padj_calc <- pmin(df$P_raw * (m / df$Rank), 1)
df$padj_final <- rev(cummin(rev(df$padj_calc)))

## Built-in R function
df$R_function <- p.adjust(df$P_raw, method = "BH")

df





Low-count genes → difficult to achieve statistical significance
Pre-filtering → reduces total number of tests n → increases statistical power
Cases where padj is NA in DESeq2::results():

Low-count gene (excluded by independent filtering)
Outlier gene (based on Cook’s distance)

text:
2. Visualization of DEG Results






Notedownload practice data



save the following files in data/ in your R project



File
Link




dds_DESeq2.rds
📥 Download






##| eval: false

dds <- readRDS('data/dds_DESeq2.rds')

res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "Tumor", "Normal"))


MA Plot (Global View)
















X-axis: Mean Average (A), Y-axis: Log Ratio (M = log₂FC)
Check for data bias and LFC inflation in low-count genes
Should be symmetric around Y=0
apeglm::lfcShrink(): controls LFC in low-count genes (recommended)


##| eval: false
## MA plot
plotMA(res, ylim = c(-10, 10), main = "Before Shrinkage")

## LFC shrinkage (apeglm)
library(apeglm)
resLFC <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "condition_Tumor_vs_Normal", type = "apeglm")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plotMA(res, main = "Before Shrinkage", ylim = c(-5, 5))
plotMA(resLFC, main = "After Shrinkage (Recommended)", ylim = c(-5, 5))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))



Volcano Plot (Gene Selection)






X-axis: log₂(Fold Change), Y-axis: −log₁₀(adjusted p-value)
Identify genes with large |LFC| and low p-value


##| eval: false

library(ggrepel)

res_df <- as.data.frame(resLFC) %>%
  rownames_to_column("gene_id") %>%
  mutate(is_significant = padj < 0.05 & abs(log2FoldChange) > 1)

p_thr <- 0.05; lfc_thr <- 1
vol_data <- res_df %>%
  mutate(diffexpressed = case_when(
    log2FoldChange > lfc_thr & padj < p_thr ~ "UP",
    log2FoldChange < -lfc_thr & padj < p_thr ~ "DOWN",
    TRUE ~ "NO"
  ))

ggplot(vol_data, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj),
                     color = diffexpressed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("DOWN" = "blue", "NO" = "grey", "UP" = "red")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-lfc_thr, lfc_thr), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(p_thr), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text_repel(data = head(arrange(vol_data, padj), 10),
                  aes(label = gene_id), color = "black") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Volcano Plot",
       x = "Log2 Fold Change", y = "-Log10 Adjusted P-value")



Heatmap (Pattern Inspection)






Visualize expression patterns of top significant genes
Inspect patterns between Case/Control and identify outlier samples
Apply vst/rlog transformation → z-score scaling


##| eval: false

library(pheatmap)

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)

## Top 20 DEGs
top_genes <- res_df %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(log2FoldChange))) %>%
  head(20) %>%
  .$gene_id

mat <- assay(vsd)[top_genes, ]
df <- as.data.frame(colData(dds)[, c("gender", "condition")])

pheatmap(mat,
         scale = "row",            ## z-score
         show_rownames = TRUE,
         show_colnames = FALSE,
         annotation_col = df,
         cluster_cols = TRUE,
         main = "Top 20 DEGs Heatmap")

title: W8. DEG Results Processing
section: 📝 W8 Assignment: Simple vs. Paired Model
text:
📝 W8 Assignment: Simple vs. Paired Model

1. Comparing the Number of DEGs

Simple model (~ condition): ~17,000 DEGs
Paired model (~ patient + condition): ~15,700 DEGs

From a variance decomposition perspective: the paired model accounts for patient effects separately, so patient variance that was incorrectly attributed to condition in the simple model is now partitioned out. As a result, some genes lose significance, but the remaining DEGs are more likely to reflect true biological signal.


2. Gold Standard Genes
Validate the change in p-values between models using known LUAD marker genes such as TOP2A, SFTPA1, SFTPB, SFTPC, and AGER.


3. Volcano Plot with Highlight

##| eval: false

## Highlight specific genes
highlight_genes <- c("TOP2A", "SFTPA1", "SFTPB", "SFTPC", "AGER")
highlight_data <- vol_data %>% filter(gene_id %in% highlight_genes)

ggplot(vol_data, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj),
                     color = diffexpressed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("DOWN" = "blue", "NO" = "grey", "UP" = "red")) +
  geom_point(data = highlight_data, color = "purple", size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(data = highlight_data,
                  aes(label = gene_id), color = "purple") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Volcano Plot (Paired Model)",
       x = "Log2 Fold Change", y = "-Log10 Adjusted P-value")

title: W11. Vibe coding tips
W11. Vibe coding tips
W11. Vibe coding tips
section: The three ingredients of a prompt
text:
The three ingredients of a prompt
A good prompt = role + context + a specific request

A bad prompt
Do some statistics for me
→ The AI has no idea what you want. You get something useless.


A good prompt (revisit your prompt engineering every 3–6 months!!)
You are a clinical biostatistician.

I am writing a paper on SBRT in patients with oligometastatic disease.
The data frame df_pt has the following variables:
- Age_Tx: age at treatment (continuous)
- Sex: sex (M/F)
- Primary: primary site (Colon, Rectum, Lung, etc.)
- Death: death (0/1)
- OS: overall survival (months)
- size_cm: tumor size (cm)
- PTVmean_BED10: mean PTV BED10 (Gy)

Write R code that does the following:
1. Build Table 1 with gtsummary (compare groups by Death, include p-values)
2. Relabel the variables with publication-ready labels
3. Save it to results/Table1.docx






TipTips for writing prompts




Paste the output of colnames(df) — the AI has to know your exact variable names
State the variable types — continuous / categorical / survival time
Specify the output you want — “save as Word”, “tiff at 300 dpi”, “forest plot”, and so on
Name the packages — “with gtsummary”, “with survminer”, etc.

title: W11. Vibe coding tips
text:
A realistic workflow
In practice, vibe coding looks like this:
1. Load the rds file in RStudio
2. Paste the AI's code into the console and run it
3. Error → paste the error message back to the AI → get fixed code
4. Check intermediate results (head, str, plot, ...)
5. Once you are happy with it, save it as a .R file
6. You end up with a script that has a clear input → output structure
The key is not trying to write a perfect script from the start. Run things line by line in the RStudio console, keep troubleshooting the intermediate steps, and only save to a file once the code actually works.


① Load the data in RStudio and inspect its structure

library(tidyverse)

indir  <- "examples/analysis/"
outdir <- "examples/analysis/"
resdir <- "examples/results/"

df_pt <- readRDS(paste0(indir, "w11_2_df_pt_processed.rds"))

# Copy this output and paste it to the AI
colnames(df_pt)
str(df_pt)




② Write the prompt
Paste the output of colnames() and str(), then ask for the analysis you want.
Run a survival analysis on the data above.

- Kaplan-Meier curve: based on Death/OS, comparing groups by Multiplicity (single vs multiple)
- Show the log-rank test p-value on the plot
- Include a risk table
- Use the survminer package
- Save as a 300 dpi tiff



③ Run the AI’s code in the console
Paste the generated code into the RStudio console and run it one block at a time.
The code will most likely arrive in the function + main structure we saw above.
In that case, do not run main() right away — run the function definitions first, then test the functions one by one.

library(survival)
library(survminer)

# Kaplan-Meier fit
fit <- survfit(Surv(OS, Death) ~ Multiplicity, data = df_pt)

# KM curve
p <- ggsurvplot(
  fit,
  data = df_pt,
  pval = TRUE,
  risk.table = TRUE,
  xlab = "Time (months)",
  ylab = "Overall survival",
  palette = c("#2E86AB", "#A23B72"),
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)

print(p)




④ What if you get an error?
Just paste the error message verbatim to the AI.
I ran this code and got the following error:

Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE) : 
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 54, 0, 108

Please fix it.
→ The AI spots that Death is a factor, so Surv() cannot use it
You keep repeating run → error → paste to AI → fix.






ImportantThe trap of mindlessly pasting errors



When something breaks, it is tempting to throw it straight at the AI. But spending 30 seconds checking it yourself first is far more efficient.
Why? The AI forgets earlier context as the conversation gets longer. Paste an error → the AI patches part of it → another error → paste again… repeat that and code that started out clean turns into a patchwork mess. You take the long way round to a fix that could have happened in one step.
What to try first when you hit an error:
# 1. If you don't know the function, read its help page
?survfit
?ggsurvplot
?tbl_summary

# 2. In RStudio you can also search the function name in the Help tab
#    → the Arguments section tells you what each argument expects
#    → the Examples section shows real usage










Just skimming the Arguments section is often enough to catch things like “ah, this argument wants a number and I gave it a string”.
A concrete example:
# Error from the AI-generated code
ggsurvplot(fit, pval.coord = "top-right")  # Error!

# ?ggsurvplot → pval.coord takes a numeric vector c(x, y)
ggsurvplot(fit, pval.coord = c(0.1, 0.1))  # fixed ✅
If you filter the problem yourself first and then ask, the AI answers with the right context and the fix lands on the first try.








TipWhat to do when you hit an error




Read the error message — find out which function failed
Check usage with ?function_name — argument types, required vs. optional
If you still can’t tell — give the AI the error and what you found in ?function_name

I got an error with this code:
[error message]

Looking at ?ggsurvplot, pval.coord seems to take
a numeric vector — how should I fix this?
Asking this way makes it far less likely that the AI guesses wrong.




⑤ Once it works, save it as a script
When everything runs in the console, collect the code into a .R file. State the input and output at the top, and tidy up the paths with paste0().

# ===== 03_KM_plot.R =====
# Input:  analysis/2_df_pt_processed.rds
# Output: results/KM_OS.tiff, results/KM_OS.pdf

# ----- directories -----
indir  <- "examples/analysis/"
resdir <- "examples/results/"

library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(survminer)

# 1. Load data
df_pt <- readRDS(paste0(indir, "w11_2_df_pt_processed.rds"))

# 2. KM fit
fit <- survfit(Surv(OS, Death) ~ Multiplicity, data = df_pt)

# 3. Plot
p <- ggsurvplot(
  fit,
  data = df_pt,
  pval = TRUE,
  risk.table = TRUE,
  xlab = "Time (months)",
  ylab = "Overall survival",
  palette = c("#2E86AB", "#A23B72"),
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)

# 4. Save
tiff(paste0(resdir, "w11_KM_OS.tiff"), width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", res = 300)
print(p)
dev.off()

ggsave(paste0(resdir, "w11_KM_OS.pdf"), plot = print(p), width = 7, height = 5)

cat("✅ KM plot saved!\n")

Rscript 03_KM_plot.R






NoteWrite Input/Output at the top of the script



# Input:  examples/analysis/w11_2_df_pt_processed.rds
# Output: examples/results/w11_KM_OS.tiff, results/KM_OS.pdf
With this, you can tell what the script reads and what it produces just by opening the file later.

title: W11. Vibe coding tips
section: Statistical traps AI falls into (why domain knowledge matters)
text:
Statistical traps AI falls into (why domain knowledge matters)






Warning




Reference level direction — relevel(factor, ref = "baseline") is often left out
Patient vs. lesion as the unit — OS is per patient, LFFS is per lesion
Missing multiple-comparison correction — comparing several subgroups without Bonferroni
Missing-value handling — the default is na.rm = FALSE, so results can come back as NA
Survival time and event swapped — watch the order in Surv(time, event)

These are things a human has to know. That is exactly why we learned R syntax ourselves back in W2–W3.

title: W11. Vibe coding tips
text:
Vibe coding checklist
✅ Did you give the AI the output of colnames() and str()?
✅ Did you state the unit of analysis (patient / lesion)?
✅ Did you specify the output format? (docx, tiff, html)
✅ Did you name the packages to use?
✅ Did you check the reference level, units and p-values yourself?
✅ Did you confirm it runs in the console before saving it as a .R file?
✅ Did you write Input/Output at the top of the script?

text:
Tips: 유전자 ID 변환
RNA-seq 데이터에서 흔히 쓰이는 유전자 ID 체계:









ID 종류
예시
출처
쓰임새




Gene Symbol
TP53, EGFR
HGNC
사람이 읽기 쉬움 (중복이 있을 수 있음)


Ensembl ID
ENSG00000141510
EBI
RNA-seq 정렬 결과의 기본; 고유하고 안정적


Entrez ID
7157
NCBI
유전자 집합 라벨 (KEGG, GO)




변환 방법: org.Hs.eg.db + mapIds()

library(tidyverse)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
library(AnnotationDbi)

# Ensembl ID에서 버전 번호 제거
my_ids <- rownames(count_matrix)
head(my_ids)  # ENSG00000141510.15

my_ids <- sapply(my_ids, function(x) {
  strsplit(x, '\\.') %>% unlist %>% .[[1]]
})
my_ids <- as.character(my_ids)

# Ensembl → Symbol
my_symbol <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
                    keys = my_ids,
                    column = "SYMBOL",
                    keytype = "ENSEMBL",
                    multiVals = "first")

# Ensembl → Entrez ID (GSEA/KEGG용)
my_entrez <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
                    keys = my_ids,
                    column = "ENTREZID",
                    keytype = "ENSEMBL",
                    multiVals = "first")

# 확인
my_genes <- tibble(ids = my_ids,
                   symbol = my_symbol,
                   entrez = my_entrez)

# NA 확인 (신규 유전자, 위유전자(pseudogene), 버전 불일치 등)
sum(is.na(my_genes$symbol))
my_genes %>% filter(is.na(symbol))

2. GDC Data Portal

Analysis Center에서 특정 변수를 기준으로 생존 곡선을 그려 보세요

화면 캡처(스크린샷)를 제출해 주세요

title: W6. 탐색적 데이터 분석 (EDA)
text:
통계 분석에 들어가기 전에 데이터를 시각화해서 전반적인 특성과 품질을 파악하는 단계

품질 관리 (Quality Control): 이상치(outlier) 시료 찾아내기
배치 효과 탐지 (Batch Effect Detection): 실험 날짜, 장비 등 기술적 잡음이 생물학적 신호를 가리고 있지는 않은지 확인
이분산성 (Heteroscedasticity): 발현량이 클수록 분산도 커짐 → 발현량이 높은 소수의 유전자가 분석 전체를 좌우할 수 있음




통계 분석을 위해 RNA-seq 데이터를 변환해 주어야 합니다.











주의



vst/rlog로 변환한 값은 시각화 전용입니다. 차등 발현 분석에는 반드시 raw count를 사용하세요!









n ≥ 30 (표본이 클 때)에 적합
전체 경향(global trend) 기반 → 빠름
발현량이 높은 유전자에는 asinh 변환
















n < 30 (표본이 작을 때)에 적합
유전자별 축소 추정(shrinkage, 베이지안 추정) → 느림
count가 낮은 유전자의 잡음을 억제













노트이렇게 생각해 보세요



유전자 A (발현량 낮음):
시료 1: 1, 시료 2: 5 ➡️ logFC = log2(5/1) = 2.32 … 잡음 ↑

유전자 B (발현량 높음):
시료 1: 1000, 시료 2: 1004 ➡️ logFC = log2(1004/1000) = 0.005 … 잡음 ↓ (안정화됨)

title: W6. 탐색적 데이터 분석 (EDA)
text:
2. 시각적 탐색 (QC Part II)
시각화로 확인할 것:

그룹 간에 차이가 있는가?
이상치 시료가 있는가?
배치 효과가 있는가?







노트실습 데이터 내려받기



아래 파일을 R 프로젝트의 data/ 폴더에 저장하세요.



파일
링크




raw_counts_final.rds
📥 내려받기


meta_data_final.rds
📥 내려받기







시각화를 위한 데이터 변환

# 1. 데이터 읽기 (count table과 메타데이터) ####
countData <- readRDS('data/raw_counts_final.rds')
dim(countData)
head(countData[,1:5])

colData <- readRDS("data/meta_data_final.rds")
head(colData)
table(colData$tissue_type)

# count table과 메타데이터의 시료 ID 확인
all(colnames(countData) == colData$barcode) # TRUE 여야 함

# 팩터 수준(level) 설정 (condition)
# 기본값: 알파벳순 … 기준(ref) = Control/Normal
colData$condition <- factor(colData$tissue_type, levels = c("Normal", "Tumor")) 
colData$condition
# case / control … treatment / control … KO / control


# 2. DESeq2 객체 (dds) ####
# countData, colData, design
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = countData,
                              colData = colData,
                              design = ~ patient + condition) # condition에 따른 DEG
colData$patient = gsub('-','_',colData$patient)
dds

# 3. 사전 필터링 (잡음 제거) ####
dim(counts(dds))

head(counts(dds)[,1:4])
head(counts(dds)[,1:4]>=1)
head(rowSums(counts(dds)[,1:4]>=1))
head(rowSums(counts(dds)>=1))
rowSums(counts(dds)) %>% head

## 3-1. 발현량이 낮은 유전자 (속도와 통계적 검정력을 위해) ####
### 방법 1: 단순 기준 (전체 count < 10?) ####
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10
head(keep)
cat(paste("   Removed", sum(!keep), "low count genes.\n"))
cat(paste("   Remaining genes:", sum(keep), "\n"))
dds_filtered <- dds[keep, ]

### 방법 2: 그룹 크기를 고려 (권장) ####
# 가장 작은 그룹에서 전체 count < 10 인가?
# 예: Control(3), Case(10) -> 최소 3개 시료에서 count가 0이 아닌가?
main_condition = 'condition'
smallestGroupSize <- min(table(colData[[main_condition]]))
smallestGroupSize*0.4
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 1) >= (smallestGroupSize*0.5)
cat(paste("   Removed", sum(!keep), "low count genes.\n"))
cat(paste("   Remaining genes:", sum(keep), "\n"))
dds_filtered <- dds[keep, ]

## 3-2. 교란 요인이 되는 유전자 ####
all_genes <- rownames(dds_filtered)
head(all_genes)
# 미토콘드리아: "^MT-" 로 시작
mt_genes <- grep("^MT-", all_genes, value = TRUE)
mt_genes
# 리보솜: "^RPS|^RPL" 로 시작
ribo_genes <- grep("^RPS|^RPL", all_genes, value = TRUE)
ribo_genes
# 면역글로불린: "^IG[HKL]" 로 시작 : "IGH", "IGK", "IGL"
ig_genes <- grep("^IG[HKL]", all_genes, value = TRUE)
ig_genes
# 제외할 유전자 목록
contam_list <- c(mt_genes, ribo_genes, ig_genes)
length(contam_list)
# !: 'NOT' (부정)
keep_indices <- !(all_genes %in% contam_list)
dds_filtered <- dds_filtered[keep_indices, ]
dds_filtered
saveRDS(dds_filtered, 'dds_filtered.rds')

# 4. 분산 안정화 변환 (vst) ####
## 4-1. vst (정규화와 변환) ####
vsd <- vst(dds_filtered, blind=FALSE) 
# blind = FALSE: design을 사용 (권장), blind = TRUE: 기술적 잡음만 사용

# 결과를 눈으로 확인
vsd_data = assay(vsd)




시료 상관관계 히트맵 (Sample Correlation Heatmap)

library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)

sampleDists <- dist(t(vsd_data))
sampleDistMatrix <- as.matrix(sampleDists)
rownames(sampleDistMatrix) <- paste(vsd$condition, vsd$type, sep = "-")
colnames(sampleDistMatrix) <- NULL

colors <- colorRampPalette(rev(brewer.pal(9, "Blues")))(255)
pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix,
         clustering_distance_rows = sampleDists,
         clustering_distance_cols = sampleDists,
         col = colors)









PCA Plot

# PCA
pca_res <- prcomp(t(vsd_data))
pca_coords <- as.data.frame(pca_res$x[, 1:2])

ggplot(pca_coords, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggtitle("PCA Result") +
  theme_bw()









PCA vs. MDS














PCA
MDS




입력
원자료 행렬 (시료 × 유전자)
거리 행렬 (시료 × 시료)


목표
분산을 보존
시료 쌍 사이의 거리를 보존


방법
고유값 분해 (eigen decomposition)
좌표 재구성


장점
loading으로 중요한 유전자를 알 수 있음
다양한 거리 척도를 쓸 수 있음 (유클리드-PCA, 상관, Bray-Curtis)


활용

title: W6. 탐색적 데이터 분석 (EDA)
text:
3. 배치 효과 (Batch Effect)

실험 날짜, 시퀀싱 플랫폼, 실험자 등에서 생기는 기술적 잡음
PCA plot에서 배치 메타데이터와 함께 확인
보정 전략:

시각화용: limma::removeBatchEffect() 의 잔차(residual) 사용
통계 검정용: design matrix에 배치를 포함 (다음 주에 다룹니다)



library(limma)

mat <- assay(vsd)
mm <- model.matrix(~condition, colData(vsd))
mat2 <- removeBatchEffect(mat, batch = vsd$patient, design = mm)

# 배치 효과 제거 후 PCA
rv <- rowVars(mat2)
select <- order(rv, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(min(500, length(rv)))]
pca <- prcomp(t(mat2[select, ]))
percentVar <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2))

pcaData2 <- data.frame(PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2],
                        condition = colData(vsd)$condition)

ggplot(pcaData2, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  xlab(paste0("PC1: ", percentVar[1], "% variance")) +
  ylab(paste0("PC2: ", percentVar[2], "% variance")) +
  ggtitle("PCA - After Patient Effect Removal") +
  theme_bw()

title: W10. 유전자 집합 농축 분석 (Gene Set Enrichment Analysis, GSEA)
text:
2. GSEA 알고리즘

1) 입력: 순위가 매겨진 유전자 목록





순위 지표(ranking metric) 선택지:








지표
계산식
특징




log2FoldChange
그대로 사용
단순함; 효과크기에 집중


Wald 통계량 (권장)
DESeq2의 stat 열
LFC와 불확실성을 함께 반영


Pi-value
\(-\log_{10}(p) \times \text{sign}(LFC)\)
통계적 유의성을 강조









힌트어떤 순위 지표를 써야 할까?



세 지표는 서로 상관이 매우 높지만(r > 0.9), 일반적으로는:

Wald 통계량: 효과크기와 그 표준오차를 함께 고려 → 가장 균형 잡힌 선택
Pi-value: 통계적 근거가 강한 유전자를 강조
가장 좋은 방법: 세 가지를 모두 돌려 비교 (민감도 분석)






2) 농축 점수 (Enrichment Score, ES) 계산
순위 목록을 따라 걸어가면서 각 유전자 집합에 대해 누적합(running sum) 을 계산합니다.

순위 1번부터 N번까지 모든 유전자를 훑으면서:
  → 경로에 포함된 유전자를 만나면:  누적합 += 1/K  (K = 경로 크기)
  → 경로에 없는 유전자를 만나면:    누적합 -= 1/(N-K)

ES = 누적합이 0에서 가장 크게 벗어난 값 (KS 통계량)
ES의 패턴:





발현이 증가한 경로:   ^^^^^^^\_____  → 위쪽에서 정점
무작위 (농축 없음):   ~/\/\/\/\/\/\  → 0 근처에서 진동
발현이 감소한 경로:   _______/^^^^^  → 아래쪽에서 정점



3) 통계적 유의성: 순열 검정 (Permutation Test)





1. 실제 데이터에서 ES를 계산
          ↓
2. 시료 라벨을 1,000번 무작위로 섞음
          ↓
3. 무작위 ES 1,000개 생성 → 귀무분포 구축
          ↓
4. 관측된 ES가 귀무분포에서 어디에 위치하는가?
NES (정규화 농축 점수, Normalized Enrichment Score): \[NES = \frac{ES_{observed}}{\text{mean}(ES_{random})}\] 경로 크기 차이를 보정 → 경로들 사이를 공정하게 비교할 수 있음
FDR (q-value): \[\text{FDR} = \frac{N_{>NES\text{ in random}}}{N_{>NES\text{ in observed}}}\]
